newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia watchdog says systematic poll violations.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia watchdog says systematic poll violations.

text.p: Indonesia's Independent Election Monitoring Committee (KIPP) said it had found evidence of systematic violations of general election rules during its monitoring of Thursday's poll.

KIPP, a group of leading dissidents and government critics, said its 8,000 volunteers in 47 cities in 17 provinces had found instances of multiple voting, intimidation of party witnesses, discrimination in the treatment of voters and various procedural irregularities.

"There is an indication that there was a systematic violation of the rules due to the fact that the election was organised by the bureaucracy," KIPP chairman Gunawan Mohamad told a new conference called on Friday to release the group's preliminary findings.

The four million members of the Indonesian Civil Service Corps are all members of the ruling Golkar party, which had won more than 73 percent of the vote after 96 million of the possible 125 million votes had been counted.

"KIPP volunteers found that unregistered persons were permitted to vote, party witnesses were forced to leave the polling stations and as a result the counting process lacked transparency," the body said in its report.
"There were incidents of violence and disruption near several polling stations and some KIPP volunteers were not allowed to observe the election process," the report said.

The body was critical of the computerisation of the election process and making the election database available only to the president and vice-president, armed forces chief, home affairs minister and information minister.
Indonesian Information Minister Harmoko is the head of Golkar.

"The (other) party leaders, however, do not have access to the database and therefore there is no independent check on its accuracy. There is generally a lack of transparency in all aspects of the election," the report said.
The report said the overwhelming victory for Golkar could be a reflection that many votes could have been deliberately spoiled by individual voters as a form of protest.
"An organised boycott of the election was not allowed. Thus, there was not organised means by which people could indicate their discontent with the electoral system," it said.

Gunawan, former editor-in-chief of the banned Tempo magazine, said the size of the protest vote, known as Golput or white group, was "very, very significant" and higher than the three percent obtained by the split Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI).
"There are indications that the number of spoiled ballots has increased significantly," he said.
Officials admit to around half of the 10 percent of uncast votes in the 1992 poll being deliberately spoiled.
Gunawan said changes to this year's election including a willingness among people to resist the government and the collapse of the PDI.
"I feel the significant change is the increasing courage of people to resist government pressure and express their dissent. The destruction of the PDI is the other change," Gunawan said.
